The Threespot eelpout Lycodes rossi exhibits a strikingly slow life history for a fish of its size, with all developmental milestones tied to the cold, stable thermal environment of its benthic habitat. In laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 0.8 °C [T = 0.8 °C], the incubation period from fertilisation to the hatching of the yolk-sac larva lasts 169 days [ab = 169 days], an exceptionally protracted embryonic duration that reflects the pronounced metabolic suppression imposed by near-freezing temperatures. Newly emerged prolarvae are remarkably small, possessing a wet weight at birth of merely 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of 2.5 mm recorded for this species. This lecithotrophic stage, during which the larva subsists entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, extends for several weeks before the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition to active feeding marks a critical ecological bottleneck, as the tiny mouth gape of the early larva constrains prey size and foraging success during this vulnerable period.

The transition to sexual maturity in L. rossi occurs only after several years of slow somatic growth, a pattern typical of high-latitude marine fishes with low metabolic rates. Under the same thermal regime of 0.8 °C [T = 0.8 °C], individuals attain puberty at approximately 1095 days after hatching [tp = approximately 1095 days after hatching], a duration that corresponds to roughly three full years of post-hatching development. The total length at which this reproductive milestone is achieved is 13.5 cm [Lp = 13.5 cm], representing a size that is less than half of the species' ultimate potential. The delayed onset of gonadal activity is likely an adaptive response to the unpredictable food supply and the energetic challenges of reproduction in deep, cold waters where metabolic costs must be carefully balanced against limited prey availability, resulting in a maturation schedule that prioritizes somatic safety over early breeding.

Adult body size in the Threespot eelpout shows a clear upper boundary, with the largest individuals reaching a maximum recorded total length of 32.5 cm [Li = 32.5 cm]. This ultimate length is accompanied by an asymptotic wet weight of roughly 181 grams [Wwi = roughly 181 grams], representing the maximum somatic mass attainable by the species under natural conditions. The length-weight scaling observed across the population conforms to the general allometric pattern described for zoarcid fishes, with the relationship indicating relatively deep-bodied morphology at larger sizes. At a constant temperature of 0.8 °C [T = 0.8 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for this species extends to 4745 days [am = 4745 days], a value that places it among the longest-lived members of the family Zoarcidae. This exceptional lifespan underscores the extremely slow pace of life history evolution in this polar-adapted benthic predator, where senescence is delayed and reproductive output is spread across many seasons, with the oldest wild-caught specimens exceeding thirteen years of age.

Reproductive output in L. rossi is low but consistent, matching the pattern typical of an iteroparous, cold-water species with high maternal investment per offspring. Each spawning event typically yields a small number of moderately sized eggs, with clutch size reported at approximately 337 eggs per brood [N_R_i = approximately 337 eggs per brood]. This modest fecundity, combined with the lengthy incubation period and the minute size of the newly hatched larvae, reflects a life history strategy in which survival of individual offspring is prioritised over numerical output. The large-yolked eggs provide substantial endogenous nutrition, enabling the prolarvae to develop through the critical early phases before encountering patchy prey fields on the deep continental shelf, thereby enhancing recruitment success in an environment where food is both scarce and unpredictable.

Comparative physiological data for L. rossi place it among the most extreme K-selected species within the Zoarcidae, with its life history parameters representing a clear endpoint on the slow-fast continuum. The massive age at birth of 169 days [ab = 169 days] at 0.8 °C [T = 0.8 °C] is among the longest incubation periods recorded for any Arctic marine teleost, highlighting the profound influence of temperature on embryonic development rates. The total length at puberty of 13.5 cm [Lp = 13.5 cm] represents a threshold that, once crossed, allows individuals to allocate resources toward gonadal growth without compromising somatic maintenance. This suite of traits collectively positions L. rossi as an archetypal deep-sea, cold-adapted specialist whose life history is finely tuned to the persistently low temperatures and limited food availability of its Arctic and sub-Arctic benthic environment, confirming its status as one of the most slow-growing teleosts known from polar waters.
